knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f={u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=2u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =2u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that the velocity is $v(t)=3 \csc^{2}{\left(t \right)},$ the acceleration $a(t)$ of the particle is given by the derivative of the velocity with respect to time. Find the function $a(t).$

$a(t)=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \operatorname{cot}t$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write

$$
v(t)=3{csc}^{2}(t).
$$

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
v=3{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{csc}t.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=6u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{'}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =6u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =(6\operatorname{csc}t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =-6{csc}^{2}t\operatorname{cot}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express
$$
f(x) = (\cos{(x)})^{4}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function
$$
f = u^{4}, \qquad u = \cos{(x)}.
$$

Differentiating, we get
$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm d u} = 4u^3, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin{(x)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get
\begin{align*}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt]

&= 4u^3 \cdot (-\sin{(x)})\\[5pt]

&=\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4\cos^3{(x)}\sin{(x)}}.
\end{align*}

\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=- 12 u^{2},\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- \cot{\left(x \right)} \csc{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\\&=(- 12 u^{2})\cdot(- \cot{\left(x \right)} \csc{\left(x \right)})\\&=12 \cot{\left(x \right)} \csc^{3}{\left(x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=- 6 \csc^{4}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f=- 6 u^{4},\qquad u=\csc{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=- 24 u^{3},\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- \cot{\left(x \right)} \csc{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\\&=(- 24 u^{3})\cdot(- \cot{\left(x \right)} \csc{\left(x \right)})\\&=24 \cot{\left(x \right)} \csc^{4}{\left(x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$
